Bangalore Livspace- experience is positive with us. Cost wise it’s higher or may be highest ,material used was premium great quality vs other vendor we could see the difference easily. Factory finish and only assembled/installed at home. Time bound and process oriented like IT companies. Time taking for sure . Different team will do various tasks like measuring, revalidation of measurements, designer hands over this after initial design freeze etc.. did not feel like external vendor tie up, this was during Covid era. Dealing with different teams was a bit of hassle as they lacked coordination among themselves like time schedule of visits, during Covid time business was at risk.initially you will be assigned senior experienced designer , once you make the payment you will be assigned a fresher kind  of designer which was a let down  may be they changed business model now to have external vendor concept. You will be at their mercy for the final outcome once it goes to factory for production. Any people issue with the designers or others will be same as IT way of handling ticket , etc . We decided not to go with them due to cost factors and alll this overhead issues, material used quality wise was good even though. Experience centre as we should understand is to attract customers and get business so don’t fall for that .

Suggest not go with small carpenter with unknown credentials or background of work done as sometimes they run away after payments or in the mid of the work or start demanding more money while work is in the middle..

Some vendors as  mentioned here - they will have brand label , and promote themselves with pics of various done , showcase them to you, trap you and operate with carpenters from just dial ..sometimes bad as they ask more money for unaccounted costs on their part else they will simply stop the work in the middle.they keep
House keys and don’t return also..ending up in nasty fights, threaten you with local goons. etc.

Local carpenters- skill may be excellent but will lack in other aspects like communication, repeated follow ups, no timeline commitments , becomes entirely person dependent, may get stuck in thru personal lives like  this workers marriage or too much work for them but no workers to do the work.
Local carpenters they may show catalogues and ask you to choose colors  and they focus on execution only but final output will be worse or much different or quiet opposite than what you expected.
Local carpenters will need some one local for sure while the work in progress at the apartment.
Local carpenters they don’t take care that much and boast of their expertise here..
These interior guys when they take work they will promise that they will take care of everything end to end and say little intervention wi be required .

This is electrical work, this is plumbing work and we are only interior designers , carpenter etc .. we don’t have plumber in our team, electrician will be external , we buy the material and they install… additional cut costs here will apply again.
At the end of the day it’s the end carpenter who does the actual job , the more middle men  we have more costs ..with all this pros and cons.

‼️Hand over Check list ‼️

These pointers are  more Appropriate  for inspection at the time of hand over.

Note:Carry a measuring tape and torch.
Pick something rugged for you feet and get to work󾰀

*Check if all the civil work and other modifications have been done according to what was mutually agreed upon.

*Check for seepages and cracks  in walls. 

*Tiles:Check for all tiles including flooring and walls for any cracks and chipped.

*Check for grouting.

*Check for the step in flooring between bathroom and the room adjoining it (prevents water entering the room)

*Check for bathroom floor slope towards the Nahni traps to facilitate easy drainage of water.

*Clogged drains is a common issue so check all drains.

*Tap/faucet and supply leakage( below) is a common one too.
Flush operation.

*Scratches on bathroom fittings.

*Check for the floor skirting alignment and finishing(esp in corners)

*Check for cracked ceramics 

*Doors:Gaps between door frames and wall should be sealed properly.(There will be gaps in any project)

*Check all all doors for alignment and cracks.

*Check for functioning of all hardware and signs of rusting including the door hinges.

*Check if all screws are fixed.

*UPVC window: check gaps between frame and  wall.

*Check all UPVC window shutters/balcony door for proper functionality including sliding, locking and unlocking.

*Inspect windows and glasses for scratches,cracks and residual paint.

*Electrical :Check for additional electrical points you have asked for.

*AC main switch control provision ,ALSO check for provision for outdoor units.

*Wall paint:Check wall finishing.

*Water metres:Check for installation of water metres(Usually installed at the water entry point into the flat,each flat may have 2 to 3 entry points depending on the location of bathrooms)

*RCCB/RCBO:Check if RCCB or RCBO has been installed.
{RCCB residual current circuit breaker
Principle:current flowing through an equipment shall flow back in full. 
If a Human experiences a shock-current is leaked/earthed(residual current)-doesn't flow back in full to the main-mains trip-life saved

More advanced version is RCBO (integration of earth leak and short circuit)}

Finally at the time of possession remember to take all keys󾰀

Please feel free to add points in the comments  and I will incorporate it in the main body.

 
We look  forward to a friendly and warm community.

Never use plywood for long shutters and sliding doors. Irrelevant of brand or quality of plywood, due to its core layers arrangement and glue used in it, plywood has tendency to bend in long run. Sliding door shutters must always be made of blockboard, HDHMR or aluminium profiles. Unlike plywood, blockboard is made of wooden battens and wooden veneers which gives it more strength and structural stability. These qualities make blockboard ideal product for all shutters and sliding doors.

One of my friends got it done in Tridasa after registration and found 10-15 issues in her flat which later are addressed by tridasa itself after that only they started interiors
Inspection of bare shell flat is very important before starting any kind of interiors

It's more about checking whats visually possible. Like checking installation of smoke detectors, checking doors for closing, sliding french doors for their operation, issues with tiles or kitchen granite (cracks or major scratches). Check bathroom fittings like sink and commode for any damages etc.
Also during handover probably carry a water bottle to check slopes of bathrooms, utility and balcony.
Leakage though will continue but sometimes it might be visible during handover as well and those could be major in nature which will be better handled if specified during handover.
Check AC piping if provided and are provided at the correct location (if not this may be a major work for the builder)
Check switch operations, if possible carry a good knight machine to check socket operations. (These may not be costly to get repaired by self but if there is a wiring issue then it can be complex)
Verify taps specifically mixers in kitchen and bathrooms.
These are some pointers. It's better to go with a checklist.

1. They are requesting bank to hold 5% and disburse rest.
2. Asking the owner what is left from their side to be paid by them complete.

5. From the date of complete payment confirmation they will take 20 days and give keys for interior. Not sure if this 20 days is fix or it will go more.

Sure, so here are the factors-
1. Garjan is a tree, there is no way to figure if its original and generally warranty is also less… now many people would say that they are using century 701 and so on and generally most use the sainik 701 which is the cheapest waterproof ply. They are giving green panel ply with 25 years warranty. Most people give warranty ranging from 3 to 10 years. 
2. Laminate company and width as you mentioned is crucial but which ones are covered is also important as there are multiple variants in that as well - Matt, gloss, texture, high gloss, etc … similar goes for internal laminate, they aren’t giving the traditional white base laminates but other options also like wooden, textured etc 
3. Edge bending used is of Rehau brand which is the best one available in market. Also they are providing 2 mm edge bending, generally it is 1 or 0.8 mm mostly in market - pretty safe when you have kids at home. Also, it’s not just for other shutters but internal carcass as well  
4. Hardware is the next element that drives cost - they are using Hafele soft close everywhere and Blum tandem boxes… 
5. Many people that we met were stingy on the no of design meetings and so on, they were quite flexible that way… even if the design phase takes 2 months 
6. We saw an executed project of our final choices, and felt the delivery quality and finish was much better for them… 

Now all these parameters are individual choices in the sense where one wants to spend or doesn’t that will drive the cost. In market for a 3 bhk interiors can range from 15 Lakh to 50 Lakh 😅 their execution time is also higher though basis their project value but in my experience it takes time when you have to deliver quality and not quantity. 

Hope this helps. Above is purely what we researched, noticed and deciphered.

Based on current market rates for a newly constructed 2BHK of 1,355 sq. ft. in a gated community, a base rent of ₹40,000 is appropriate. Any additional investment in interiors and appliances should be added proportionately. Floor rise premiums should also be factored in on a proportional basis. Structuring the rent this way helps maintain consistent pricing, reinforces community standards, and supports long-term property value.

For a 1,926 sq. ft. east-facing apartment on the 22nd floor with complete interiors, including ACs, geysers, and appliances, in my view, the base rent should be ₹55,000, with all additional factors such as interiors, appliances, and floor-rise premiums added proportionately on top of this base. This positioning aligns with market expectations for a premium unit and helps protect overall community and property value.

A helpline number and details of the nodal officer have also been released to facilitate the filing of complaints against those who fail to comply with these directives.

The Delhi government's move aims to bring greater transparency and accountability in schools while easing the financial burden on parents.

Given the current state of My Home Sayuk with amenities still ramping up and ongoing interior work causing noise, it might be worth considering short-term leases (4–6 months) as a practical option for this calendar year.

A few reasons why this could work better in the current phase:

• **Reduces early exits**: Tenants signing long-term leases right now may get frustrated with noise / incomplete amenities and end up leaving early anyway.

• **Better alignment**: Short-term tenants come in with the right expectations about temporary inconveniences.

• **Flexibility to increase rent later**: Once amenities are fully functional and the society settles, owners can re-rent at better market rates instead of being locked into current pricing for a year.

• **Lower vacancy / churn risk**: It’s better to have a stable short-term tenant than deal with unexpected vacancies or frequent turnover.

Overall, this is a temporary strategy to bridge the current phase while maximizing long-term rental value.

I do not believe the facilities office is restricting any owner from renting out their flat through external agents or online portals. From my understanding, the intention is primarily to ensure security within the community.

Agents visiting the society to show a particular flat should ideally visit that flat and complete their work. However, there have been instances in the past where individuals associated with property rentals were observed moving across multiple towers and visiting various flats, including units where interior works were in progress. Such situations naturally raise concerns from a security perspective.

In this context, the collection of Aadhaar details and closer monitoring of agents entering the premises appears to be a security and accountability measure rather than an attempt to prevent owners from using external rental agencies. Owners should certainly have the freedom to rent out their properties through channels of their choice, but appropriate safeguards are equally important to protect the interests of the entire community.

In my view, the facilities team’s actions are intended to address security concerns and ensure that agents entering the society can be properly tracked and held accountable if required.

I am sharing my recent experience with NextGen Interior (Nallagandla) as a strong warning to anyone considering them. Based on a friend’s recommendation, we approached them a month ago and paid a token advance of ₹50,000.

Our experience was a complete disaster from start to finish, marked by incompetence, massive price inflation, and shockingly unprofessional behavior:

**Zero Creative Inpu**t: For our 2,262 sq. ft. apartment, we were initially quoted ₹18.5 Lakhs. When design work began, it quickly became clear that the designer lacked any personal initiative or creativity. We had to spoon-feed every single requirement and spend hours managing the process ourselves, receiving virtually no professional guidance in return.

**Bait-and-Switch** **Pricing**: Once the designs were finally settled, they handed us a revised estimate of ₹27 Lakhs—a massive, unjustified leap from the initial quote. When we requested a transparent breakdown and questioned the heavily inflated itemized rates, they refused to negotiate, giving us a blunt "take it or leave it" ultimatum.

**Financial Dishonesty on Refunds**: When we chose to cancel, they explicitly agreed to refund 75% of our token money. However, they shortchanged us yet again, returning only 65% while hiding behind petty, manufactured excuses to pocket the rest.

**Hostile and Aggressive Management**: Attempting to get our rightful money back revealed the firm's true colors. **__The Managing Director, Mr. Madhu__**, became extremely hostile and verbally abusive, hurling insults (calling us "bloody idiots"), throwing the estimate papers at us, and nearly instigating a physical altercation.

Losing our hard-earned money hurts, but being cheated, insulted, and intimidated in a professional transaction is entirely unacceptable. This firm operates with zero integrity and total disrespect for clients. I strongly advise everyone to steer completely clear of NextGen Interior.

No, a builder cannot legally charge you more than what’s written in the Sale Agreement / BBA*, except for 3-4 specific situations. 

This is covered under *RERA - Real Estate Regulation Act 2016* + Indian Contract Act.

*1. When Builder CANNOT charge extra*
Once you and the builder have signed the *Agreement to Sell / Sale Agreement* with a fixed price, the builder is bound to it. 
They cannot later say: "Cement rates went up, pay 2L more" or "We added extra amenities, pay extra".

If they do, it’s a violation and you can file a complaint with *RERA*.

*2. When Builder CAN legally charge extra* 
Only these are allowed, and only if they were mentioned in the agreement:

1. *Statutory Charges / Govt Taxes*: GST, Stamp Duty, Registration, Metro cess, Property tax. These change as per govt rules and are usually kept "as applicable".
2. *Area Variation*: If final carpet area is more/less than what was in the agreement by >3-5%, then pro-rata adjustment happens. This clause should be in your agreement.
3. *Optional Add-ons*: Extra car parking, club membership, modular kitchen, higher floor premium. Only if you opted for it in writing.
4. *Delayed Payments by You*: If YOU delayed EMI to builder, they can charge interest as per agreement.

*3. Common illegal extra charges builders try*
1.  "Development charges" / "Infrastructure charges" after agreement
2.  "Legal fees" / "Documentation charges" not mentioned
3.  "Corpus fund" / "Maintenance 3 years" increased without basis  
4.  "PLC - Preferential Location Charges" added later

All of these can be challenged.

*4. What you should do if builder is demanding extra*
1.  *Check your Agreement*: Look at "Total Consideration" + "Payment Schedule" + "Any clause for escalation". If it’s not there, you don’t have to pay.
2.  *Send Written Objection*: Email/Letter: "As per Clause X of our agreement dated *, total cost is *. Any demand beyond this is not valid."
3.  *RERA Complaint*: If builder insists, file online complaint on Telangana RERA portal. Builders have been penalized for this. 
4.  *Withhold Registration*: Don’t do final registration/payment till dispute is cleared, or pay under protest and get receipt.

*Important for Telangana / Hyderabad*
Under TSRERA rules, builder must also give you the final price breakup in Form 2. Any demand beyond that needs mutual written consent.

---

*Bottom line*: Signed agreement = final price. Builder can’t unilaterally increase it.

We've our interiors finalized with Dhwaara interiors so want to share our testimonial with others.

We've went ahead with Dhwaara for our interiors, of all the vendors we've talked to dhwaara felt the most value for money and was able to quote very near to our budget. We've got our first draft of 3D designs and you can see them attached to this message. 

What led to our decision:

1. Transparency: Dhwaara was very upfront about lot of the designs, estimates and material they provide. Some of the other interior firms were dodgy with their estimations and kind of material they were using.

2. Customization: What stood out to me was their customization. My requirement was fully modular, and unlike many others who mainly try to convince you about the products or materials they offer Dhwaara actually understood our requirements and taste and designed accordingly.

3. Design philosophy: Most of the design was almost finalized in the very first set of renders itself, which was a great experience. We've shared our references before design and sat with them couple of times to explain what we wanted.

4. Earlier work: We've seen earlier work done by dhwaara in person and were impressed by how fully designed the home looked with the budget they've quoted and the materials they have used. Finishing wise things could've been bit better but the home was not fully ready by the time we've visited and these was very minor issues.

If anyone is looking for interiors, I would definitely recommend Dhwaara Interiors. They are professional, transparent, and genuinely good people to work with.
